paragraphs: Mikkelal melakot haasurot min hattora, hu hakkoteb vehammocheq; velav davqa mocheq otiyyot hu dechayyab, ella apillu machaq tishtush deyo bilbad chayyab, im yesh bimqomo liktob shette otiyyot. veim hu shiur ot achat, "p sheppatur miqqarebban chattat useqila - hare zeh asa issur min hattora, kedin chatzi shiur deasur min hattora. veim nishar beyadayv tippat deyo mechamat shehaya koteb beereb-shabbat, asur lerachetza beshabbat, ella korek aleha chatikat beged beet netila shello yabo sham mayim. veken hu haddin im yesh alayv shear tzeba deasur lerachatzu.

clarification.explanation: One of the Sabbath labors Torah-forbidden is "writing and erasing." Not only erasing actual letters carries liability, but even erasing a mere ink stain (with no letters) carries liability, if the erased area is large enough to write two letters in it. And if the area is large enough only for one letter — though exempt from a sin-offering and the penalty of stoning, one has still committed a Torah-level prohibition, following the rule that "half the measure is Torah-forbidden." One who has an ink drop left on his hands from writing on the Sabbath eve — may not wash it off on the Sabbath, but must wrap a piece of cloth around it when washing hands so water does not touch it. The same law applies to any other dye stuck to the hands — it may not be washed off.
takeaways: Erasing ink or any stain (even without letters) over an area the size of two letters is Torah-forbidden.
Erasing over an area the size of one letter is also Torah-forbidden (under the rule of "half the measure"), though it carries no penalty.
An ink or dye drop left on the hand may not be washed off on the Sabbath, but should be covered with cloth when washing hands.

paragraphs: Hakkoteb, "p deeno chayyab min hattora ella im ken koteb bedabar hammitqayyem al dabar hammitqayyem, mikkol maqom asur middibre soperim apillu bedabar sheeno mitqayyem al dabar sheeno mitqayyem. velaken asur liktob beetzbao bemashqin al hashshulchan, o lirshom al haabaq shebbazzekukit, o lirshom betzipporen al gab hanneyar; vetzarik lehizzaher name shello lirshom betzipporen al hasseper kemo sheosin lesiman lizkor ezeh dabar, v"p sheeno roshem betabnit ketab, asur.

clarification.explanation: The labor of writing carries Torah liability only when writing with a lasting substance (such as ink) on a lasting surface (such as paper). But even writing with a non-lasting substance on a non-lasting surface is rabbinically forbidden. Therefore it is forbidden to write with a finger in a beverage on the table, or to mark in dust on glass, or to mark with a fingernail on the back of paper. One must also be careful not to mark with a fingernail on a book to remind oneself of a place — even though this is not an actual letter shape, it is nevertheless forbidden.
takeaways: Writing with a non-lasting substance (a beverage, dust) on a non-lasting surface is rabbinically forbidden.
It is forbidden to mark with a fingernail on paper or a book as a reminder, even without letter shapes.

paragraphs: En tzebia baokalin; velaken muttar letabbel pitto bemashqeh hatztzabua ap al gab dehappat nitzba; veken muttar litten beokel dabar shetztzobea im en kavvanato litzboa, abal im kavvanato litzboa, asur gam baokalin, meachar dekavvanato litzboa. veap al gab deamarnu kol sheen kavvanato litzboa en issur tzebia baokalin, mikkol maqom bemayim ushear mashqin tzarik lehizzaher, "p sheen kavvanato litzboa, mishshum dedame leoseh en hatztzeba, deasur min hattora ledaat haramba"m za"l, vekaasher katabti bazeh bsh"q "rab- pealim" bs"d. velaken mah shennohagim poh irenu shemmebiim al hashshulchan bimsibba gedola shene kelim shel zekukit gedolim, umemalleim otam mayim tzebuim kegivvun shel "qaramez" leyopi venoy, sheyyihyu nirim keillu hem meleim shekar adom - shello yaaseh tzeba hammayim haellu beshabbat. veasur lehannicha "kechal" beenayim beshabbat, mishshum tzobea.

clarification.explanation: The law of "dyeing" does not apply to foods. Therefore it is permitted to dip bread in a colored beverage, even though the bread becomes colored by it; and it is likewise permitted to put into food something that causes coloring, if one does not intend to dye. But if one's intent is to dye — it is forbidden even with food, since everything depends on intent. Nevertheless, regarding water and beverages one must be careful even without intent to dye, since this resembles "creating the appearance of dye" (creating a colored look), which according to the Rambam is Torah-forbidden. For this reason, the custom at large gatherings of bringing to the table two large glass vessels full of water colored red (so they appear full of red beer — a beer-like beverage, for beauty) — one may not color this water on the Sabbath itself. Likewise it is forbidden to apply kohl (eye makeup) on the Sabbath, since this is a prohibition of dyeing.
takeaways: With food itself there is no prohibition of dyeing when there is no intent to dye, but if the intent is to dye — it is forbidden.
With water and beverages one must be careful even without intent to dye, since this is considered "creating the appearance of dye," which is Torah-forbidden.
It is forbidden to color water on the Sabbath for decoration (such as to look like red beer), and it is likewise forbidden to apply eye makeup (kohl) on the Sabbath.

paragraphs: Poh irenu darkam laasot shekar laban veshekar adom, velipamim mearebim zeh bazeh - tzerikin lizzaher shello yittenu haadom betok hallaban, ki hem nicha lehu laasot lehallaban adom, vekavvanatam lekak. veayyen "nishmat-adam", kelal d', ot g', yeuyyan sham. veayyen "eshel-abraham", seip qatan k"h, deasar bemokere yen-sarap umi-debash latet letoko tzeba kede sheyyiqnu mimmennu, mishshum denicha lehu bekak veku', yeuyyan sham. veim yaaseh lehepek, sheyyitten hallaban beadom, kemo shekkatab mahari"y chagiz za"l sheyyittenu hayyayin hallaban beadom - libbi mehasses behetter zeh beheka dekavvanato litzboa hallaban, ki im davqa beheka deen kavvanato litzboa hallaban, nireh lehattir bikhay gavna litten hallaban beadom.

clarification.explanation: In Baghdad it was customary to make white and red beer, and sometimes they are mixed together — one must be careful not to mix red into white, since here there is a genuine intent to turn the white into red, and this is considered intentional, forbidden dyeing. It was likewise observed that some forbid selling brandy and mead with added color to attract buyers, since the seller has an interest in the coloring. By contrast, if one does the reverse — pouring a white beverage into a red one (as one authority wrote) — there is doubt here: if his intent is to dye the white, it appears this too is forbidden; but if he has no intent to dye the white (for example, he only wants to add quantity), it appears one may be lenient in this case.
takeaways: Deliberately mixing red color into a white beverage in order to dye it is forbidden, since the intent is to dye.
Selling a beverage with added color to attract buyers is likewise forbidden for the same reason.
Pouring white into red without intent to dye — there is room to be lenient.

paragraphs: Asur lehaddeq bepi hapak mokin o chatikat beged keshehen lachim ubaloin min hammashqeh, denischatin "y hidduq; v"p sheeno mitkavven lekak - pesiq resha hu, v"p sheeno mehaddeq harbeh, gazeru shemma yehaddeq bechozeq. usepog, en meqannechin bo kelal, ella im ken yesh bo achiza; vaapillu chadash veyabesh asur, dela pelug rabbanan; veayyen "tosepet-shabbat", seip qatan l"b.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to wedge a piece of cotton wool or cloth into the mouth of a bottle when it is wet and soaked with a beverage, since the wedging causes the beverage to be squeezed out of it, and even though this is not his intent — this is an "inevitable certain result," and is therefore forbidden. And even if one does not wedge it forcefully, the Sages forbade it as a decree lest one come to wedge it forcefully. And a sponge — it is forbidden to clean with it at all, unless it has a handle (so it will not be squeezed during cleaning); and even a completely new, dry sponge — is forbidden, since the Sages did not distinguish between the cases.
takeaways: It is forbidden to wedge cloth or cotton wool soaked with a beverage into a bottle's mouth, since this causes an inevitable squeezing.
A sponge may not be used for cleaning on the Sabbath unless it has a handle, and even a new, dry sponge is forbidden by the Sages' general decree.

paragraphs: Im nishpak mashqin sheen melabbenim al hammappa sheal hashshulchan - hinneh hatta"z za"l oser lishob hammashqin hahem tok kap echad velishpok lachutz, d"g demashlik leibbud, mikkol maqom beshaa shehu shoeb tok hakkap oseh issur, vehave lah tolada dimpareq, velo yoil mah sheshshopek leibbud; ak harab "eliyya raba" za"l choleq al hatta"z bazeh, umattir lishob mashqin ellu sheenam melabbenim bekap vaapillu bekoach, kevan sheddato lehashlikam leibbud. vbsh"q "mqbtzl" heeleti k"eliyya rabba" za"l; abal bemashqin hammalbenim asur lishob veasur ligror apillu besakkin, mishshum degorer vedocheh hammashqin lemaqom yabesh veasur mishshum mekabbes, veod mishshum issur sechita, vaapillu im eno sochet bekoach, gazerinan shemma yischot bekoach, sheyyesh bazeh issur tora.

clarification.explanation: If a non-whitening beverage (that is, one that does not stain white, such as wine) spills on the tablecloth — there is a dispute: the Taz forbids scooping it up with a spoon and pouring it out, since even if one intends to discard it as a loss, the very act of scooping from the cloth carries a prohibition of "a derivative of extracting" (drawing liquid out of an absorbent material). The "Eliyah Rabbah," by contrast, permits scooping up such a beverage with a spoon even forcefully, since his intent is to discard it as a loss and not to benefit from it. The Ben Ish Chai rules according to the lenient view of the "Eliyah Rabbah." But with a whitening beverage (one that stains a white color, such as milk) — it is forbidden to scoop it up or scrape it even with a knife, since scraping it pushes the beverage toward a dry area and this is considered "laundering" (whitening cloth), and additionally there is a prohibition of squeezing involved — and even without intent to squeeze forcefully, there is concern one might come to squeeze forcefully, which carries a Torah prohibition.
takeaways: A non-whitening beverage spilled on a tablecloth — permitted to scoop up with a spoon and discard (following the lenient view the Ben Ish Chai rules by).
A whitening beverage (such as milk) — forbidden to scoop or scrape from the cloth, due to the prohibitions of laundering and squeezing.

paragraphs: Yesh nohagim, keshennapal tinnup al malbush vekaddomeh, yirchatzu oto beopen zeh - sheyyaabiru alayv hammayim, o yenaneu oto bemayim ad sheyyusar hattinnup, velo yischatu oto, ella yannichuhu ad sheyyibash; vesoberim shemmuttar bekak, mechamat deen sochatin oto; ubeemet hu issur gamur, vezeh taut beyadam, shehu melaka gemura, ken katab haramba"m za"l biktibat yad, vehebio beresh seper "maaseh-roqeach". veim hishtin tinoq al habbeged, lo yishpeku alayv mayim kede lebattelo, dishriyyato zehu kibbuso; veken lo yesannen mayim bachaluqo, abal mappa hamyuchedet lekak, shari.

clarification.explanation: Some are accustomed, when dirt falls on a garment, to rinse it with water or shake it in water until the dirt is removed, without wringing it out, and let it dry on its own — and they think this is permitted since they are not actually wringing it. But this is a complete error — it is fully forbidden and constitutes the actual labor of laundering, as the Rambam wrote. And if an infant urinated on a garment, it is forbidden to pour water on it to remove the stain, since "its soaking is its laundering" (soaking in water is considered actual laundering). Likewise it is forbidden to filter water through an ordinary garment (such as a robe), but it is permitted to filter through a cloth specially designated for filtering.
takeaways: Rinsing a dirty garment with water without wringing it out is still considered laundering and is entirely forbidden — a common mistake.
It is forbidden to pour water on a garment an infant urinated on, since the soaking itself is considered laundering.
Filtering water through an ordinary garment is forbidden; through a cloth specially designated for filtering — it is permitted.

paragraphs: Hassear en bischitato issur min hattora, mippene shehassear qasheh veeno bolea hammayim betoko; ak sechitat sear asura middibre soperim. vehattobel beshabbat - ben ish, ben ishah - lo yischatu hassearot shellahem, ella yabiu mitpachat gedola hamyuchedet leniggub veyitnaggebu bah, viqannechu bah penehem verosham. v"g d"y haqqinnucha nischat hassear - have sechita kilachar yad, vekevan dischitat sear derabbanan, hittiru bikhay gavna dei epshar, mishshum dehave kilachar yad, vehammayim hannischatin holekin leibbud; veim kol zeh lo yeqanneach bekoach, ella benachat leat leat ad sheyyibleu hammayim shebbassear bemitpachat. veyesh chasidim sheen mequnnachim sheyyaarot hazzaqan, ella menappetzim oto beyadam, veyannichu shettitnaggeb hallachluchit meeleha. vekaasher shoteh haadam mayim o shear mashqin, nakon lehizzaher lebilti yischot sear hassapa beyado, ella yeqanneach bemitpachat; veayyen tosepet shabbat, seip qatan t"l umehachitztzit hashsheqel, seip qatan k"g.

clarification.explanation: Wringing hair is not Torah-forbidden, since hair is hard and does not absorb water into itself (water only clings to its outside), but nevertheless wringing it is rabbinically forbidden. Therefore one who immerses on the Sabbath — man or woman — should not wring out his hair, but should bring a large towel designated for this and dry himself with it, wiping his face and head with it as well. And even though this wiping squeezes out a bit of the hair's water, this is considered "indirect squeezing" (in a roundabout, not direct, manner) — and since wringing hair is only a rabbinic prohibition and cannot be entirely avoided, this was permitted, especially since the squeezed-out water is lost. Nevertheless, one should not wipe forcefully but gently and slowly, until the water absorbed in the hair is gradually absorbed into the towel. Some pious individuals are stringent and do not wipe their beard hair at all, but only shake it with their hands and let the moisture dry on its own. Likewise, when a person drinks a beverage, one should be careful not to squeeze the mustache hair with one's hand, but wipe with a towel.
takeaways: Wringing hair is rabbinically forbidden (not Torah-forbidden); therefore it is permitted to dry with a towel gently, even if a little hair-water is squeezed out incidentally.
One should dry slowly and gently, not wipe forcefully.
It is advisable not to squeeze mustache hair by hand after drinking, but rather wipe with a towel.

paragraphs: Basar chay, apillu eno malucha, muttar letaltelo mippene sherauy laakilat adam, sheyyesh bene-adam kosesin basar chay; abal basar qasheh sheeno rauy lekos oto, asur letaltelo; vehu haddin shumman vekayyotze, deen rauy leakelo chay, deasur letaltelo; v"g derauy liklabim vachatulim, kol sherauy lemaakal adam eno omed lakkelabim; abal basar sarucha muttar letaltelo, dehu rauy lakkelabim veomed liklabim; veayyen shulchan aruk rabbenu zalman, siman sh"ch, seip s"ch. vbsh"q "mqbtzl" heeleti, dehay dina debasar chay muttar betiltul mishshum dachaze leumtza, lo shayyak bazzeman hazzeh, ki atta anachnu roin delekka bene-adam benenu shekkosesin basar chay. veken dag malucha muttar letaltelo, vesheeno malucha asur, sheeno rauy leshum adam, veeno omed lehashliko liklabim. vegam al din zeh katabti sham, dehaynu davqa bedag malucha sherauy laakila, kemo dagim meluchim habbaim meir betzara, sheddarkam lemalecham melicha mealleya harbeh shehem reuyim laakila, abal dagim shemmolechim otam meat bishbil letaggenam baesh, deen reuyim laakila kelal, asur letaltelam beshabbat.

clarification.explanation: Raw meat, even if not salted, may be handled on the Sabbath, since it is fit for human consumption — some people eat raw meat. But hard meat unfit for this — may not be handled, and likewise fat and the like unfit for raw consumption — may not be handled, even though it is fit for dogs and cats, since as long as it retains fitness for human consumption, it is not considered "designated for dogs." But rotten meat, entirely unfit for a person — may be handled, since it truly is designated for dogs' food. Rabbi Yosef Chaim adds a novel point: the ruling that raw meat may be handled because it is fit for "umtza" (raw eating) does not apply in our time, since nowadays there are no people among us who actually eat raw meat. Likewise, salted fish may be handled, and unsalted fish may not, since it is unfit for anyone and is not designated to be thrown to dogs — but this applies specifically to fish salted with a genuine salting (until it is fit for eating, such as Basra fish), and not to fish salted only slightly for frying, which is entirely unfit for eating and forbidden to handle.
takeaways: Raw meat may be handled only if fit for raw consumption (and per the Ben Ish Chai's conclusion, there are no raw-meat eaters in our time, so raw meat is muktzeh nowadays).
Fat or hard meat unfit for raw consumption — forbidden to handle, even if fit for animals.
Genuinely salted fish (fit for eating) may be handled; fish salted only lightly for frying — forbidden.

paragraphs: Betza shennoleda beshabbat, asura apillu betiltul. veim kopeh aleha keli shello tishshaber, yizzaher shello yigga bah. uperot shennasheru min hailan beshabbat, asurim apillu betiltul, vaapillu sepeqan asur.

clarification.explanation: An egg laid on the Sabbath — is forbidden even to handle, under the law of muktzeh, since it was not fit before the Sabbath began. If one covers it with a vessel so it will not break, one must be careful not to touch the egg itself while covering it. Likewise, fruits that fell from the tree on the Sabbath — are forbidden even to handle, and even if there is doubt whether they fell on the Sabbath or earlier, one should be stringent and forbid them.
takeaways: An egg laid on the Sabbath is muktzeh, forbidden to handle; it is permitted to cover it with a vessel without touching it.
Fruits that fell from a tree on the Sabbath are forbidden to handle, even in a case of doubt.

paragraphs: Haroqeq barucha veharucha mepazzer haroq – asur, mishshum dedame lezoreh; v"g deen mitkavven lekak - pesiq resha hu veasur midderabbanan. v"g deyesh choleqim al zeh - rabbo haacharonim za"l dechayeshi lazeh.

clarification.explanation: One who spits into the wind and the wind scatters the spittle — is forbidden, since this resembles the labor of "winnowing" (separating things by means of wind). And even though he does not intend to scatter the spittle, this is an "inevitable result of the act," and is therefore rabbinically forbidden. Although some disagree with this, most later authorities were stringent about it.
takeaways: It is forbidden to spit into the wind when the wind scatters the spittle, since this resembles winnowing.
Even without intent, this is an inevitable result and forbidden, and most authorities were stringent about it.

paragraphs: En olin bailan - ben lach, ben yabesh - veen nitlin bo, veen mishtammeshin bo shum tashmish, kegon lehannicha alayv chepetz o littol mimmennu chepetz, o liqshor bo behema o chebel vaarisa shel tinoq vekayyotze bazeh, hakkol asur. veim yesh chebel qashur bailan, asur litlot shum dabar beoto hachebel. umuttar liga beilan ubilbad shello yenidennu. veim yesh sal taluy bailan dehave tzedadin, asur liqqach dabar min hassal, abal im yesh yated taqua bailan vehassal taluy bayyated, dehave tzidde tzedadin, muttar liqqach dabar min hassal, abal lo yiqqach et hassal atzmo.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to climb a tree (whether living or dry) on the Sabbath, and it is forbidden to hang from it, and it is forbidden to use it in any manner — such as placing an object on it, taking an object from it, tying an animal, a rope, or an infant's cradle to it, and the like — all of this is forbidden. If there is a rope tied to the tree, it is forbidden to hang anything on that rope. It is permitted only to touch the tree itself, provided one does not shake it. If there is a basket hanging directly on the tree (called "first-degree attachment"), it is forbidden to take anything from it; but if there is a peg driven into the tree and the basket hangs on the peg (called "second-degree attachment," further removed), it is permitted to take an object from inside the basket, but forbidden to take the basket itself.
takeaways: It is entirely forbidden to climb, hang from, or use a tree on the Sabbath in any way.
It is permitted only to touch the tree without shaking it.
An object fixed directly on the tree — forbidden to touch; an object hanging through an intermediary (such as a peg) — permitted to take what is inside it, but not the object itself.

paragraphs: Lipamim hayyeladim notenim chittim vekayyotze beqarqa hechatzer kede sheyyitzmechu - tzarik ligor bahem "p shehem notenim zeh bechol, mippene shebbene habbayit baim al yede kak lide mikshol beshabbat, sheshshopekim mayim beqarqa hechatzer velav addatayhu. velaken kol adam sheroeh tzemachim bachatzero, yitlosh otam bechol, kede shello yabou lemikshol beshabbat. gam darkam shel yeladim laasot kis male chittim, veqosherim oto sabib keli cheres qatan shel mayim, kede sheyyaaleh hakkis asabim sebibot hakkeli - tzarik ligor bahem ulebattel zeh, kede shello yabou bazeh lide mikshol beshabbat, shemmetaltelin oto hakkeli mimmaqom lemaqom, vezeh dino keatzitz naqub deasur letaltelo. veatzitz shebbo natua asabim, "p sheeno naqub asur litlo meal gabbe qarqa ulehannicho al gab yetedot, dedame letolesh; veken en litlo meal gabbe yetedot ulehannicho al haqqarqa, dedame lenotea.

clarification.explanation: Sometimes children put wheat or seeds in the courtyard ground so they will sprout — one should reprimand them even if they did so on a weekday, since this causes household members to stumble on the Sabbath (they pour water on the plants in the courtyard ground without noticing it is the Sabbath). Therefore anyone who sees plants in his courtyard should uproot them on a weekday, to prevent stumbling on the Sabbath. Likewise, children accustomed to hang a bag full of wheat around a small earthenware vessel containing water, so the wheat sprouts around the vessel — should be reprimanded and this should be stopped, since household members might handle this vessel from place to place on the Sabbath, and its law is that of a "perforated flowerpot" (a pot with a hole), which is forbidden to handle. A flowerpot in which plants are grown, even if unperforated (with no hole at the bottom), may not be lifted from the ground and placed on pegs (since this resembles uprooting, detaching it from the ground), and it is likewise forbidden to bring it down from pegs and place it on the ground (since this resembles planting).
takeaways: Plants children grew in the courtyard should be uprooted on a weekday, to prevent the stumbling block of watering on the Sabbath.
A water vessel with wheat sprouting around it has the law of a perforated flowerpot — forbidden to handle on the Sabbath.
A flowerpot with plants — forbidden to move between ground and pegs, even if unperforated, since this resembles uprooting or planting.

paragraphs: Kerikat hammitznepet al hakkoba, derek qippulam, beshabbat - asar harab haggaon "shaar-asher" qubu za"l, siman t', mishshum metaqqen mana beshabbat. ubammaptechot sham hebi saad lidbarayv min chiddushe dinim lerabbanay yerushalayim haqqadmonim, yeuyyan sham. vbsh"q "rab- pealim" heerakti birayot berurot deim oseh haqqippulim umetaqqen hammitznepet al hakkoba achar shellobesho berosho, "p dikrika zo tzarik lah ummanut shettihyeh mekuvvenet yapeh - la chashib zeh metaqqen mana, ella derek lebisha hu, shehu metaqqen lebusho alayv kederek shehu choger chagoro yapeh. vehammitznepet deayyre bah chiddushe dinim hannizkar, darkam haya litchob hakkoba bikli echad sheqqorin "qlb" ("rosh", etz legihutz kobaim), umesim otah lepanayv, vekorek alayv hammitznepet beqippulim shonim beseder yapeh verauy, velaken machze kimtaqqen mana, deeno oseh zeh al gupo kede sheyyihyeh chashib derek malbush. veken hamminhag pashut poh irenu letaqqen hammitznepet al rosham beshabbat, "g ditzrika kerikatah ummanut yadayim; ubaddorot sheqqademu hayu rob anshe hair lobeshim mitznepet kazo.

clarification.explanation: Wrapping the turban (a type of head covering) around the cap in folds on the Sabbath — Rabbi "Sha'ar Asher" forbade this, out of concern for "repairing a vessel" on the Sabbath. However, the Ben Ish Chai, in his book "Rav Pe'alim," elaborates with proofs that if the folds are made and the turban arranged on the cap after it is already worn on the head — even if the wrapping requires skill and precision — this is not considered "repairing a vessel," but is the normal manner of dressing, like a person tightening his belt neatly. By contrast, the case the earlier authorities discussed was different: there it was customary to place the cap on a special implement (a "qalab" — a wooden hat-block for pressing hats) and set it down before them, and then wrap the turban around it in arranged folds — and this indeed is considered "repairing a vessel," since it is not done on the body but on an external implement, and is therefore not considered the manner of dressing. The plain custom in Baghdad was to arrange the turban on the head itself on the Sabbath, even though it requires skill, and most people of the city wore such a turban in previous generations.
takeaways: Arranging the turban on the head itself (while worn) is considered the normal manner of dressing and is permitted, even if it requires skill.
Arranging the turban off the head, on an external implement (such as a hat-block) — is considered repairing a vessel and is forbidden.
The accepted custom in Baghdad was to be lenient and arrange the turban on the head on the Sabbath.

paragraphs: Medichin kelim letzorek hayyom, vaapillu belel-shabbat letzorek shacharit; ak achar seuda shelishit asur, dehave letzorek chol. ukele shetiyya muttar lehaddicha kol hayyom, dachazu leh bekol et. vetzarik lehazhir haam behatztzaat hammittot shemmatztziim mibbeod yom letzorek hallayla, bime haqqayitz sheddarkam lehatztzia al haggag kede shettitqarer, deasur lemebad hake. vehammazhir vehannizhar, tabo alehem beraka.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to wash dishes for eating that same day, even on Sabbath night for the morning meal of the following day. But after the third meal (the last meal of the Sabbath) — it is forbidden to wash dishes, since this is now for the sake of the coming weekday and not for the Sabbath. Drinking vessels, by contrast, may be washed at any time throughout the day, since they are fit for use at any moment. The public should be warned regarding preparing beds in advance for the night: in summer it was customary to set out beds on the roof so they would cool before sleeping — and it is forbidden to do this (that is, to actually move or prepare the beds on the Sabbath itself for this purpose). One who warns the public about these matters, and one who is careful with himself — blessing will come upon them.
takeaways: It is permitted to wash dishes for that day's eating, but not after the third meal (since that is already for the sake of the coming weekday).
Drinking vessels may be washed at any hour throughout the Sabbath.
Beds may not be prepared or moved on the Sabbath itself for the purpose of cooling (such as moving them to the roof) — this is considered preparing for the weekday.
